title: 'What Do You Need Wednesday?' -- The Honesty Edition
author: The Beacon
summary: Pass A roundup. The Beacon's monthly 'What Do You Need Wednesday' edition curates four items on academic honesty, framed around the newsletter's Stripe of the Month theme of Honesty. The curator's editorial position is that peer culture outperforms surveillance culture in building high-integrity environments, and that honesty is a developmental capacity built through relationships and transparency -- not primarily through policy. Item 1 is a recommendation of James Lang's Cheating Lessons (2013), which draws on cognitive theory to argue that cheating happens for understandable reasons in specific environments and is best addressed by modifying those environments to motivate genuine learning -- a framework the curator notes presciently predicts the AI era. Item 2 presents 2026 Pew Research data showing that nearly two-thirds of U.S. teens now use AI chatbots and nearly 60% report AI-assisted cheating is common at their school -- a qualitative shift from the Stanford post-ChatGPT data showing cheating rates held steady in 2024. Item 3 introduces Canadian researcher Sarah Elaine Eaton's 'post-plagiarism' framework, which argues that AI integration has fundamentally changed what authorship means, requiring schools to have explicit rather than assumed conversations with students. Item 4 closes with Errol Morris on truth as quest. Each item includes a 'Try this' classroom activity grounding the roundup in actionable pedagogy.
points: The Pew 2026 data marks a qualitative shift from the Stanford post-ChatGPT data: cheating rates held steady in early post-ChatGPT surveys, but by 2026 students are actively deciding every day whether crossing the line costs them anything -- the culture has shifted.

Lang's Cheating Lessons argues presciently that future cheating will still happen for understandable reasons in specific environments -- making environment design, not detection technology, the durable academic integrity intervention.

Eaton's 'post-plagiarism' framework is not an endorsement of AI-assisted work but a call to recognize that authorship itself has changed, requiring schools to put explicit integrity conversations on the syllabus rather than in the handbook.

The APA's guidance treats academic integrity as a learning goal to be named explicitly in the course -- not a policy to enforce -- a reframe that shifts the locus from surveillance to developmental instruction.

The roundup's consistent pedagogical move is to invite students into the honest conversation: 'Where does AI help you learn, and where does it learn for you?' -- treating integrity as a capacity to build, not a rule to police.
quotes: Two threads run through most of the credible research on honesty: peer culture tends to outperform surveillance culture in building high-integrity environments, and honesty itself is a developmental capacity built through things like relationships and transparency.

The future of cheating may look different in terms of the specific forms it takes, but I am firmly convinced that cheating in the future -- like cheating in the past and in the present -- will happen for understandable reasons, in response to a specific environment, and can best be addressed through thinking hard about that environment.
Their data showed cheating rates among high schoolers held surprisingly steady post-ChatGPT. When students do cheat, it's driven by conditions far more than tools.

More recently, 2026 Pew Research survey found that nearly two-thirds of U.S. teens now use AI chatbots, with more than half using them for schoolwork and about 30% doing so daily. Nearly 60% say AI-assisted cheating is common at their school.
Students aren't confused about the line. They're deciding, every day, whether crossing it costs them anything.
Students' engagement with AI has evolved faster than educators' engagement with honesty as a teachable skill. The gap between those two curves is where the work lives.
Truth, I like to remind people -- whether we're talking about filmmaking, or film journalism, or journalism, whatever -- it's a quest.
